verification.passage_check: Independently re-read all 22 pages of the pinned arXiv v2 PDF, including the Section 2 oracle-search figures and Table 1, the complete learned-controller method and Tables 2-4, Appendix A, the MCTS definition and Algorithm 1 in Appendix B, all in-distribution and OOD Tables 5-10, and Appendix D's deduplication, training, parameter, and prompt details. Rechecked every one of the 12 original findings and 7 evaluations against its cited page, repaired evaluation context labels, and added missed audits for the partly definitional oracle-scaling claim and OOD subjects where MindSkip exceeds POLAR.
verification.competitor_check: Re-searched current primary literature and opened the authoritative records on 2026-08-23 for the same-author CoLa precursor arXiv:2507.07996 v1, Dr.LLM arXiv:2510.12773 v2/ICLR 2026, MACRO arXiv:2608.05872 v1, Router-Tuning arXiv:2410.13184 v6, FlexiDepth arXiv:2503.23798 v3, Mixture-of-Recursions arXiv:2507.10524 v3, Inner Thinking Transformer arXiv:2502.13842 v2, Universal Transformers arXiv:1807.03819 v3, Looped Transformers arXiv:2409.15647 v5, and the official PMLR 267 ICML 2025 PuDDing paper. Titles, dates, versions, relationship, and concrete differences were checked rather than inherited from the first review.

question: Can a lightweight learned controller improve a frozen LLM by predicting, before execution, an input-specific ordered program of contiguous layer segments that may be skipped or repeated, and do oracle-discovered programs support the claimed accuracy, efficiency, and out-of-distribution benefits?

key_findings.claim: The diagnostic MCTS results establish an oracle existence result, not a deployable inference result: each candidate program is rewarded using that same input's ground-truth answer.
key_findings.evidence: The search defines validity as producing the known correct answer and uses the binary reward r(pi,x)=1{F_pi(x)=y} during per-input simulation. Consequently, Table 1's large gains measure whether ground-truth-guided search encountered at least one correct path among many trials; the learned POLAR predictor must be evaluated separately.

key_findings.claim: Within that oracle search, skip and recurrence are complementary and joint search is much stronger than either alone, but the magnitude is dominated by answer-aware selection over programs.
key_findings.evidence: Across every DART-Math row in Table 1, Loop exceeds Skip and Skip&Loop is best. For example, Qwen2.5-3B on DM-2 rises from 13.9% under the standard path to 34.2% with Skip, 46.0% with Loop, and 76.6% with Skip&Loop; LLaMA-3.2-3B on DM-1 rises from 37.7% to 85.0%. These are search-discovery rates under the ground-truth reward rather than predictions from the learned controller.

key_findings.claim: Many MCTS-discovered correct paths use less computation than the standard forward pass, including some paths that correct an initially wrong answer.
key_findings.evidence: Among inputs already correct under the base path, 71.9% admit a shorter valid program; among initially wrong inputs for which search finds a correction, 34.0% admit a shorter correcting program. The conditioning on successful search and access to labels means these percentages are evidence of path redundancy and possibility, not an achievable online rate.

key_findings.claim: The searched paths show a strong local structural bias that motivates the practical packed-segment representation.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports that 57.7% of discovered segments contain one layer, more than two-thirds contain at most two consecutive layers, non-consecutive segments account for under 2.9%, and most segments are repeated no more than once. POLAR therefore caps contiguous segment length at four and implements only skip, keep, or one repeat.

key_findings.claim: The practical predictor does not realize the paper's fully general finite-sequence definition of a program of layers.
key_findings.evidence: The formal definition permits an arbitrary variable-length sequence of layer indices, while the implemented decoder partitions the original depth order into contiguous segments of at most four layers and assigns each segment skip, keep, or exactly one adjacent repeat. This restriction is empirically motivated but excludes arbitrary permutations, long jumps, and deeper recurrence.

key_findings.claim: POLAR predicts the entire restricted execution program before running the frozen LLM, using semantic input features and global layer-context attention.
key_findings.evidence: A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encodes the input; learnable layer queries cross-attend to token embeddings, a cross-layer transformer communicates across depth, and two heads predict boundary and operation logits. Thresholding plus constrained beam search yields ranked candidate programs trained from MCTS-valid traces.

key_findings.claim: The learned predictor improves held-out DART-Math accuracy at pass@1, so its central benefit is not limited to oracle MCTS or output sampling.
key_findings.evidence: On LLaMA-3.2-3B, POLAR pass@1 scores 54.6, 32.3, 32.7, 29.7, and 26.9% on DM-1 through DM-5, versus 48.9, 29.4, 30.4, 28.6, and 26.6% for one stochastic base sample. The gains are positive but small on DM-4 and DM-5, and no repeated-run uncertainty is reported.

key_findings.claim: The reported pass@k gains show useful candidate diversity, but monotonic pass@k is mathematical by construction and the comparison does not equalize execution cost.
key_findings.evidence: POLAR's macro-average on LLaMA rises from 35.1% at pass@1 to 51.2% at pass@5, while base sampling rises from 32.8% to 43.8%. Because pass@k is the probability that any of the first k candidates succeeds, it cannot decrease as k grows; and each POLAR candidate executes another layer program, while no matched-FLOP or matched-latency top-k comparison is reported.

key_findings.claim: The oracle-search test-time-scaling result is partly definitional, and the paper's wording about the accuracy of valid programs is internally inconsistent with its own validity definition.
key_findings.evidence: A program is defined as valid exactly when it yields the correct answer. Expanding a nested recurrence/search space can only preserve or increase the chance that MCTS encounters at least one valid program, so Figure 5(a)'s monotonic discovery curve does not by itself show that extra latent computation causally improves a fixed policy. Figure 6 is described as increasing the 'average accuracy of valid execution programs,' even though every valid program has binary accuracy one by definition; the paper does not clarify whether the plotted population is all searched programs, best programs, or inputs with a discovered path.

anchors.section: Appendix B.1-B.3 / validity and binary reward

key_findings.claim: A mathematics-trained controller transfers positively to the reported OOD tasks, but the evidence is one benchmark suite without statistical uncertainty or contamination controls.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, POLAR improves ASDiv from 59.1 to 63.8%, MAWPS from 41.7 to 46.7%, and every listed MMLU-Pro subject over the greedy base. Similar appendix tables cover the other backbones. The paper offers a semantic-embedding and simple-program explanation, but does not isolate those factors or report seeds, confidence intervals, or pretraining-overlap audits.

key_findings.claim: POLAR does not outperform prior dynamic-depth methods on every OOD subject, despite the paper's broad conclusion language.
key_findings.evidence: In Table 8 for LLaMA-3.2-3B, MindSkip exceeds POLAR on several MMLU-Pro groups, including Physics (47.7 versus 39.0), Chemistry (43.3 versus 41.0), Philosophy (49.7 versus 44.5), and History (55.6 versus 48.8). In Table 10 for Qwen3-8B, MindSkip also wins on Chemistry (31.5 versus 23.4), Law (58.0 versus 48.7), Other (67.0 versus 57.1), Philosophy (68.5 versus 56.7), and additional subjects. POLAR is broadly strong and improves the greedy base, but superiority over every prior router is false at the subject-cell level.

key_findings.claim: The pass@1 latency experiment supports a speed improvement on one 24-layer model, although the resource accounting is narrower than the complete routing system.
key_findings.evidence: On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the paper assigns 3.05 ms to the encoder, predictor, and beam search, and reports 311.41 ms at 23.30 average layers on DM-1 versus 373.45 ms for the 24-layer base (0.83x), and 353.31 ms at 23.76 layers on DM-5 (0.95x). The 2.1M-parameter footprint counts the learned predictor but not the separately required frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.

key_findings.claim: The current revision repaired duplicate-question leakage in the in-distribution split, which is important negative evidence about earlier results.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix states that arXiv v2 deduplicates DART-Math questions within each difficulty level before the train/validation/test split and reruns affected in-distribution analyses. The authors say qualitative conclusions remain unchanged and OOD results are unaffected, but do not tabulate the pre/post revision deltas.

anchors.section: D.1 / revision note and split counts

key_findings.claim: The MCTS-to-supervision pipeline is not reproducible from the paper alone, and its multiple-valid-program supervision is underspecified.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix gives symbolic MCTS quantities N_sim, exploration constant c, and length penalty lambda but no numerical values, random seed, per-input search budget, beam width, or complete program-target selection rule. The training text says multiple valid programs may exist and only explains down-weighting the full-depth trace when a shorter one exists, leaving the handling of conflicting segment labels unclear.

anchors.section: B.2-B.3 / symbolic search constraints and UCB

method.core_idea: Treat the frozen transformer's ordered layers as callable functions, use answer-aware MCTS offline to discover correct skip/repeat paths, compress the observed path structure into bounded contiguous segments, and train a small controller to predict an input-specific full execution program before the base LLM runs.
method.mechanism: For diagnostics, MCTS starts from the standard layer sequence and applies bounded contiguous Skip or Repeat actions, scoring complete paths with the input's ground-truth answer. For deployment, a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B provides token features; learnable layer queries cross-attend to those features and pass through a depth-wise transformer. Boundary and operation heads predict a partition of the base layers into segments of length at most four and label each segment skip, keep, or repeat once. Boundary thresholding and a small operation beam search produce top-k candidate programs, which are executed on an otherwise frozen LLM. Binary cross-entropy trains boundaries and masked cross-entropy trains operations using offline MCTS-valid programs.
assumptions: Per-input paths found with access to the correct answer reveal exploitable latent computation rather than multiple-testing artifacts over a huge path space.
MCTS traces discovered on the training distribution provide learnable supervision for unseen inputs without leaking answer-specific search behavior.
When several paths are valid for one input, the chosen or weighted segment labels define a stable target rather than mutually inconsistent supervision.
Short contiguous segments and at most one repeat preserve the useful portion of the much larger arbitrary layer-sequence space.
A frozen general-purpose embedding model exposes the input difficulty and semantics needed to select a base-LLM execution path.
Program candidates ranked by local operation likelihood and a small beam approximate the globally best interacting layer composition.
Comparisons to skip-only and routing baselines use sufficiently matched training data, tuning, and program budgets.
Best-of-k program execution and best-of-k output sampling are meaningful without an explicitly equalized FLOP or latency budget.
A single difficulty-wise split and the reported deterministic run are representative without confidence intervals or repeated seeds.
Question-text deduplication within each difficulty eliminates all material DART-Math train/test contamination and templated near-duplicate leakage.
OOD gains reflect transferable computation control rather than benchmark familiarity in the base LLM or semantic embedding model.
The 2.1M learned-head count and measured encoder latency adequately represent the deployment cost of requiring a separate 0.6B embedding model.
Direct final-answer prompting is sufficient to generalize conclusions about latent reasoning beyond short-form benchmark inference.
Accuracy changes caused by nonstandard layer order reflect useful computation rather than uncalibrated activation-distribution shifts that happen to alter the decoded answer.

techniques.role: Searches per-input layer paths offline and labels a path valid only when it produces the known answer.
Edits the standard layer sequence through bounded deletion or adjacent duplication of layer blocks.
Represents the practical program as original-order segments of at most four layers.
Assigns each segment one of skip, keep, or exactly one repeat.
Uses frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B token features to condition routing independently of base-LLM hidden states.
Builds one input-conditioned representation per layer index by querying the input token embeddings.
Coordinates boundary and operation decisions using global depth context.
Learns binary segment starts and masked categorical operations from parsed valid paths.
Ranks several complete operation assignments after deterministic boundary decoding.
Measures whether any of the top-k predicted execution paths returns the correct answer.
Splits each DART-Math difficulty after exact question-text deduplication in the v2 revision.

evaluations.setting: DART-Math DM-1 through DM-5 on four frozen LLMs under per-input MCTS (pp. 3-5, Section 2 and Table 1; pp. 14-15, Appendix B and Algorithm 1)
evaluations.metric: Fraction of inputs for which answer-aware search discovers a correct path within Skip, Loop, or joint Skip&Loop spaces
evaluations.result: Joint Skip&Loop is best in all 20 model-by-difficulty rows; examples include LLaMA DM-1 37.7 to 85.0% and Qwen2.5 DM-2 13.9 to 76.6% relative to the standard path
evaluations.baseline: Standard fixed path, skip-only search, and loop-only search; all search variants use the same input's ground-truth answer as reward

evaluations.setting: MCTS-discovered successful programs across models and DART-Math difficulty (pp. 3-5, Section 2 and Figures 3-7)
evaluations.metric: Total executed depth, unique-layer depth, segment locality, and recurrence count
evaluations.result: 71.9% of base-correct inputs and 34.0% of corrected base-wrong inputs have a shorter valid path; 57.7% of segments are single layers, over two-thirds are at most two consecutive layers, and non-consecutive segments are under 2.9%
evaluations.baseline: The original full-depth, each-layer-once forward pass

evaluations.setting: Held-out, deduplicated DART-Math with LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct (pp. 7-8, Sections 4.1-4.2, Table 2, and Figure 8)
evaluations.result: At pass@1, POLAR scores 54.6/32.3/32.7/29.7/26.9% across DM-1 to DM-5 versus 48.9/29.4/30.4/28.6/26.6% for one base sample; at pass@5 its gains over base sampling are +9.3/+5.7/+8.1/+6.6/+7.4 points
evaluations.baseline: Greedy base, temperature-tuned base sampling, ShortGPT, MindSkip, FlexiDepth, and DR.LLM

evaluations.setting: Held-out DART-Math on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen3-8B (pp. 17-19, Appendix C.1 and Tables 5-7)
evaluations.metric: pass@5 accuracy across five difficulty levels
evaluations.result: POLAR's per-level gains over base sampling are +15.6 to +17.5 points on Qwen1.5, +13.5 to +40.4 on Qwen2.5, and +9.9 to +23.4 on Qwen3
evaluations.baseline: Temperature-tuned base sampling and four dynamic-depth baselines at the same k, without a matched total-execution-cost report

evaluations.setting: Zero-shot transfer after training on the union of DART-Math training levels (pp. 8-9, Section 4.3 and Table 3; pp. 19-20, Appendix C.2 and Tables 8-10)
evaluations.metric: pass@1 exact-answer accuracy on ASDiv, MAWPS, and 13 MMLU-Pro subject groups
evaluations.result: For Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, POLAR improves ASDiv 59.1 to 63.8%, MAWPS 41.7 to 46.7%, and every listed MMLU-Pro group; appendix tables report broad gains for the other models
evaluations.baseline: Greedy full-depth base, ShortGPT, MindSkip, FlexiDepth, and DR.LLM

evaluations.setting: Single-model wall-clock study on 24-layer Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2 and Table 4)
evaluations.metric: Component overhead, average executed layers, end-to-end latency, and relative accuracy gain
evaluations.result: Routing components total 3.05 ms; DM-1 uses 23.30 layers and 311.41 ms (0.83x base, +5.7 points), while DM-5 uses 23.76 layers and 353.31 ms (0.95x base, +9.4 points)

evaluations.setting: DART-Math data audit in arXiv v2 (p. 21, Appendix D.1)
evaluations.metric: Exact question deduplication and difficulty-wise train/validation/test counts
evaluations.result: After deduplication, DM-1 through DM-5 contain 565/1,349/1,579/1,537/1,577 examples, totaling 4,130 train, 826 validation, and 1,651 test; affected experiments were rerun and the authors report unchanged qualitative conclusions
evaluations.baseline: The earlier arXiv evaluation protocol that split duplicate response records before this correction

evaluations.setting: Subject-level OOD comparison on LLaMA-3.2-3B and Qwen3-8B (pp. 19-20, Appendix C.2 and Tables 8 and 10)
evaluations.metric: pass@1 exact-answer accuracy for 13 MMLU-Pro subject groups
evaluations.result: POLAR improves the greedy base broadly, but MindSkip is higher on LLaMA Physics (47.7 versus 39.0), Chemistry (43.3 versus 41.0), Philosophy (49.7 versus 44.5), and History (55.6 versus 48.8), and on Qwen3 Chemistry (31.5 versus 23.4), Law (58.0 versus 48.7), Other (67.0 versus 57.1), and Philosophy (68.5 versus 56.7)
evaluations.baseline: MindSkip and the greedy full-depth base; the mixed wins are negative evidence against universal superiority over prior dynamic-depth methods

limitations: Author-disclosed: the practical program space bounds segments at four layers and one repeat because richer paths are rare in MCTS traces; it does not implement the arbitrary finite layer sequences allowed by the formalism.
Author-disclosed: the arXiv v2 evaluation had to remove duplicate DART-Math questions before splitting and rerun the in-distribution results; exact pre/post correction deltas are not shown.
Author-disclosed: experiments focus on mathematical reasoning and related benchmark transfer; robustness, calibration, interpretability, and safety in high-stakes settings remain future work.
Reviewer-identified: MCTS uses the true answer on the same input as its reward, making Table 1 and path-existence claims oracle search upper bounds subject to a large multiple-comparison surface.

Reviewer-identified: the paper does not report numerical MCTS simulations, exploration constant, length penalty, random seed, search cost, beam width, or enough trace-selection details to reproduce the supervision corpus.

Reviewer-identified: multiple valid programs can assign conflicting boundaries and operations, but the loss description does not fully specify target aggregation or sampling beyond down-weighting the full-depth trace.
Reviewer-identified: pass@k is nondecreasing by definition, and top-k program candidates are not compared with output sampling under matched FLOPs, layer executions, energy, or latency.

Internal-contradiction audit (reviewer-identified): Figure 6 describes varying average accuracy among 'valid' programs even though validity is defined as producing the correct answer; the evaluated population is not specified clearly enough to reconcile the terms.
Reviewer-identified: all accuracy tables omit repeated seeds, uncertainty intervals, statistical tests, and sensitivity to split or controller initialization.
Reviewer-identified: the OOD tests do not audit whether the pretrained base or embedding models saw benchmark questions or close templates.

Reviewer-identified: the claimed 2.1M controller size excludes the required frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; only its measured latency, not its model footprint or memory cost, enters the efficiency discussion.
Reviewer-identified: latency is reported for one model and lacks hardware, batch-size, warm-up, generation-length distribution, memory, and variance details needed to generalize the speedup.

Reviewer-identified: several adapted skipping baselines collapse to near-zero accuracy, but their tuning budgets and compatibility adaptations are not described in enough detail to establish a fair comparison.

Negative-result audit (reviewer-identified from Tables 8 and 10): MindSkip outperforms POLAR on multiple LLaMA and Qwen3 MMLU-Pro subjects, so the broad claim to outperform prior dynamic-depth methods is not uniform.

Reviewer-identified: Base sampling reports the best test result over temperatures 0.3, 0.7, and 1.0 without stating a validation-only temperature-selection protocol, while top-k sampling and top-k program execution are not compute matched.

Reviewer-identified: direct final-answer prompting on short benchmarks does not test long generation, KV-cache behavior, tool use, conversational state, or whether path changes remain stable token by token.
Reviewer-identified: there is no activation-distribution, calibration, or safety audit for repeatedly applying layers outside the order on which the base model was trained.
Reviewer-identified: statements that fixed depth captures only a narrow subset of latent reasoning capacity overreach evidence that selected alternative paths can change benchmark answers.
failure_modes: MCTS discovers a correct answer by chance after many answer-aware trials, but no label-free controller can identify that path on a new input.
Multimodal valid-path supervision averages incompatible routes into boundary and operation predictions that correspond to no valid program.
The semantic embedding router learns dataset, template, or difficulty-level identity instead of transferable computation requirements.
Exact-question deduplication leaves paraphrases or problem-family templates split across train and test.
A high-ranked skip/repeat program shifts hidden-state scale or position outside training support and becomes brittle under small prompt changes.
Best-of-k accuracy improves only because k separately executed programs spend more total compute, eliminating the claimed efficiency advantage.
The external 0.6B embedding model dominates memory or serving complexity even when the learned head is small.
Layer savings fail to yield wall-clock savings under batching because different examples follow heterogeneous execution paths.
Program rankings or accuracy gains disappear across random seeds, alternative splits, or a new MCTS supervision sample.
Routing policies trained with direct-answer prompts fail when generation is long and the appropriate path changes across output tokens.
A path that improves exact-match accuracy worsens calibration, refusal behavior, toxicity, or robustness because safety-relevant late layers are skipped.
The constrained packed-segment decoder misses the rare nonlocal or multi-repeat paths needed for the hardest inputs.
Baseline routers are under-tuned or mis-adapted, making POLAR's relative advantage larger than a matched implementation would show.
OOD gains reflect memorized benchmark content in Qwen3-Embedding or the base LLM rather than domain-general execution control.
reusable_insights: Separate oracle path-existence experiments from label-free routing accuracy; the former can map architectural redundancy without being presented as deployable performance.
Use structural statistics from expensive search to compress a combinatorial execution space before learning a controller.
Predicting an entire path up front can coordinate decisions across depth and avoid sequential routing overhead.
Represent original-order contiguous layer blocks as modules when search traces empirically show strong locality.
Compare skip, repeat, and joint operators to determine whether compute removal and compute reuse are complementary.
Report both total layer applications and unique layers because recurrence increases the former without changing the latter.
Deduplicate by semantic problem identity before any split, not only by exact response record or exact question string.
For best-of-k methods, match total executed layers, FLOPs, latency, and energy rather than matching k alone.
Include every auxiliary encoder in parameter, memory, initialization, and serving-cost accounting.
Train path prediction with set-valued or distributional supervision when many execution programs are valid for the same input.
Measure repeated-seed route stability and answer stability, not only mean task accuracy.
Audit skipped and repeated paths for calibration and safety regressions before treating dynamic execution as an efficiency-only change.
open_questions: At matched total layer executions, does predicted-program search still beat ordinary output sampling and self-consistency?
How many MCTS simulations per input were used, and how do discovery rates scale with that oracle search budget?
Can a set-valued objective learn the full distribution of valid paths better than independent boundary and operation losses?
Do the same routes remain valid across paraphrases, decoding seeds, and small prompt-format changes?
How much of routing accuracy remains with a much smaller encoder, base-model early hidden states, or simple difficulty features instead of Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B?
Do semantically deduplicated or newly generated math problems reproduce the reported gains?
What is the Pareto frontier under matched wall-clock latency, peak memory, energy, and batch throughput?
Does up-front routing work for long autoregressive generations where the required computation may change by token?
Can paths be verified for activation scale, calibration, and safety before execution?
Which layer segments are consistently skipped or repeated across tasks, and do they have a mechanistic interpretation?
Does allowing two or more repeats, noncontiguous modules, or limited reordering help hard inputs enough to justify the larger decoder space?
How does POLAR compare with the later MACRO controller under identical models, search data, and compute budgets?
Can label-free self-evaluation replace ground-truth-rewarded MCTS when constructing route supervision?

competitive_landscape.title: Skip a Layer or Loop it? Test-Time Depth Adaptation of Pretrained LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct same-author precursor that introduces answer-aware MCTS over skipped, repeated, and reordered pretrained layers on a per-sample basis.
competitive_landscape.difference: The precursor establishes oracle chain-of-layers existence and reports shorter/correcting paths but still searches each test example; POLAR's substantive addition is a learned up-front segment-program predictor intended to amortize that search.

competitive_landscape.title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior learned-router competitor, also trained from MCTS supervision to skip, execute, or repeat frozen pretrained blocks.
competitive_landscape.difference: Dr.LLM makes sequential local decisions from intermediate hidden states and repeats individual layers; POLAR predicts the whole route before execution and operates on bounded contiguous segments. This narrows POLAR novelty to coordination and representation rather than learned skip/repeat routing itself.

competitive_landscape.title: MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct post-publication competitor current at the review date that learns distributions over layer skips, repeats, and residual-add moves without changing base weights.
competitive_landscape.difference: MACRO uses a context-dependent Markov policy and top-k Viterbi decoding and reports a 9.4x route-search reduction plus gains over Dr.LLM; POLAR instead uses semantic input cross-attention and a bounded packed-segment program. A matched comparison is absent because MACRO appeared after POLAR.

competitive_landscape.title: Router-Tuning: A Simple and Effective Approach for Enabling Dynamic-Depth in Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior lightweight dynamic-depth method and the source of the MindSkip baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: Router-Tuning learns attention-based per-token layer skipping for efficiency and does not repeat blocks; POLAR jointly skips and repeats input-level contiguous segments and targets accuracy as well as cost, but depends on expensive offline oracle traces.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive Layer-skipping in Pre-trained LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior plug-in routing method for token-dependent layer skipping in a frozen pretrained LLM and the source of the FlexiDepth baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: FlexiDepth adds routers and adapters to vary layers by generated token and reports that irregular routes do not yet yield wall-clock speedup; POLAR predicts one input-level route before generation, permits repetition, and reports latency on one model.

competitive_landscape.title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest trained recurrent-depth architecture combining shared parameters with token-level adaptive recursion.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mixture-of-Recursions trains a recursive transformer and token routers jointly and changes active-token attention and KV caching; POLAR retrofits fully frozen standard layer stacks and repeats pretrained contiguous segments, avoiding base training but offering weaker token-level adaptation.

competitive_landscape.title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior recurrent-depth model that routes difficult tokens through extra internal thinking steps.
competitive_landscape.difference: Inner Thinking Transformer requires architecture-aware training, residual thinking connections, token routing, and step encodings; POLAR uses existing frozen layers and an external controller, trading native recurrent training for retrofit convenience.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational adaptive recurrent-depth transformer with shared computation and a halting mechanism.
competitive_landscape.difference: Universal Transformers are designed and trained around recurrent transition blocks with per-position adaptive computation; POLAR instead composes heterogeneous layers from a pretrained conventional stack and does not retrain those layers.

competitive_landscape.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior evidence that repeated transformer computation and inference-time loop counts can improve algorithmic length generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: Looped Transformers train a shared block for controlled recurrence and study length extrapolation; POLAR repeats selected segments of an ordinarily trained pretrained LLM and studies math-answer accuracy and execution cost.

competitive_landscape.title: Prompt-based Depth Pruning of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior prompt-conditioned up-front routing method, published as PuDDing at ICML 2025.
competitive_landscape.difference: PuDDing trains a lightweight prompt router to choose the best layer-omission set from a data-derived option library before the LLM executes. It cannot repeat segments or synthesize POLAR's bounded operation programs, but it means that prompt-based one-shot depth selection predates POLAR; the remaining novelty is coordinated joint skip/repeat segment composition and its MCTS-derived representation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first practical program-of-layers framework that jointly skips and repeats pretrained LLM layer modules, predicts a complete input-specific program in one shot, improves accuracy over standard and prior dynamic-depth inference while often executing fewer layers, and transfers out of distribution.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Its practical system combines offline MCTS trace discovery, a bounded contiguous-segment representation, a frozen semantic input encoder, global cross-layer coordination, and constrained beam decoding; experiments cover four LLMs, five DART-Math difficulty levels, arithmetic OOD tasks, MMLU-Pro subjects, and one latency study.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The same-author CoLa precursor already established oracle skip/repeat path search, Dr.LLM already learned skip/execute/repeat routing from MCTS traces, and the ICML 2025 PuDDing paper already predicted a prompt-specific layer-omission choice before execution. The credible novelty is therefore narrower: globally coordinated prediction of packed contiguous-segment programs that jointly support skipping and repetition, plus the revised multi-model evaluation. Claims about broad latent reasoning capacity, monotonic test-time scaling, universal baseline superiority, and efficiency must be narrowed because oracle search uses labels, pass@k and nested-space discovery are definitionally nondecreasing, execution budgets are not matched, routing supervision is underspecified, several OOD subject cells favor MindSkip, uncertainty is absent, and the auxiliary 0.6B encoder is excluded from the headline parameter count. MACRO, posted in August 2026, is a direct later alternative for full-route decoding and further limits any continuing uniqueness claim.

reviewer_notes: Secondary verification independently re-read the complete 22-page pinned arXiv v2 extraction, including MCTS definitions and Algorithm 1, every main and appendix table, the training configuration, direct prompt, and the duplicate-question revision note. All original findings, anchors, evaluations, novelty statements, limitations, negative results, and contradiction audits were checked passage by passage; two missed tensions were added: oracle scaling is partly a nested-search/definition effect, and MindSkip wins several appendix OOD subject cells. The exact local PDF/text hashes and 22-page bound match fulltext_index. Ten closest primary records were checked at explicit current versions on 2026-08-23, including the newly added official ICML 2025 PuDDing record and later MACRO v1. Confidence is high about the method and transcription, but not absolute because the paper omits numerical MCTS/search settings, route-target aggregation, beam width, repeated seeds, and reproducible latency conditions. The verified reading consistently separates answer-aware oracle path existence from deployable learned-controller performance.
